title: One in 15 Million: Brisbane Mother Delivers Identical Quadruplets Sharing a Single Placenta
excerpt: Jenitar Na'amoana, 34, gave birth to four genetically identical girls at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital in what doctors describe as an unprecedented monozygotic quadruplet pregnancy.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Brisbane mother Jenitar Na'amoana gave birth to identical quadruplets on July 14.
  • Identical quadruplets occur in approximately one in 15 million pregnancies.
  • The babies, born at 28 weeks, are recovering in the NICU.
  • A GoFundMe campaign for the family has raised over 39,000 AUD.
  • The Na'amoana family now has eight children after this rare birth.

  • Jenitar Na'amoana, a 34-year-old Brisbane mother of four, gave birth to naturally conceived identical quadruplet girls on July 14 at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital.
  • Identical quadruplets occur in roughly one in 15 million pregnancies, and doctors say it is "unheard of" for all four babies to share a single placenta.
  • The babies — Emily, Harriet, Catherine, and Alexa — were delivered via caesarean section at 28 weeks and four days and are recovering in the NICU.
  • A GoFundMe campaign for the family, which now has eight children, has raised over 39,000 Australian dollars.

A Brisbane woman has given birth to identical quadruplet girls in a pregnancy so rare that doctors estimate the odds at one in 15 million — and possibly even longer, given that all four babies shared a single placenta.

Jenitar Na'amoana, 34, and her husband Jortham, who were already parents to four children, welcomed Emily, Harriet, Catherine, and Alexa via caesarean section on July 14 at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital in Herston, Queensland. The babies were delivered at 28 weeks and four days of gestation.

A Medical Rarity

Dr. Alexa Bendall, the specialist who oversaw Na'amoana's care, told the BBC that monozygotic quadruplets — where a single fertilized egg splits into four genetically identical embryos — occur in approximately one in every 15 million pregnancies.

"It's unheard of for the babies to share the same placenta. So the fact that we've got four beautiful, healthy babies born at 28 weeks and four days is incredible."

— Dr. Alexa Bendall, Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital

The conception occurred naturally, without fertility treatments. In such cases, a single egg is fertilized by a single sperm and then divides four times to produce four separate but genetically identical embryos. The fact that all four shared one placenta — known as monochorionic — adds an additional layer of medical rarity and risk.

A High-Risk Pregnancy

Monochorionic multiple pregnancies carry elevated risks, including twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and unequal nutrient distribution through the shared placenta. Na'amoana's medical team monitored the pregnancy closely.

"We always said that if we could get her to 28 weeks, we would be doing well," Bendall said. Na'amoana carried the babies through that milestone with no major complications, which her doctors described as remarkable.

The four girls, born premature, are currently in the neonatal intensive care unit at the hospital, where they are expected to remain for several weeks as they grow stronger. Both mother and babies are reported to be doing well.

Family of Eight

The birth has doubled the Na'amoana family's number of children from four to eight, a reality that has brought both joy and logistical challenges.

"Our four precious miracles have arrived safely," Na'amoana wrote on a GoFundMe page set up to help cover the cost of a larger vehicle, baby essentials, and medical expenses. "And while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges we never could have imagined."

As of July 20, the GoFundMe campaign had raised more than 39,000 Australian dollars, roughly 27,000 U.S. dollars, from supporters worldwide.

Historical Context

Identical quadruplets are among the rarest events in obstetric medicine. The most famous case in medical literature is the Genain quadruplets, born in the 1930s in the United States, all of whom were later diagnosed with schizophrenia — a case that contributed significantly to research on the genetic basis of mental illness.

The last set of quadruplets born at Brisbane's Mater Mothers' Hospital, a neighboring facility, was in 2018. However, those were not monozygotic.

For members of the Australian diaspora community and families following the story, the Na'amoana birth has become a feel-good counterpoint to heavier news cycles. The family has not indicated any plans for media appearances beyond their GoFundMe updates.
